list.listitem: Ethylene glycol toxicity should be suspected in patients presenting with altered mental status and possible/unknown substance ingestion. C
Diagnostic laboratory tests should include arterial blood gases, serum chemistries, anion gap, and osmolal gap calculations, and serum ethylene glycol, methanol, and isopropyl alcohol levels. C

Treatment is generally supportive with the use of bicarbonate for the reversal of acidosis. C Fomepizole and ethanol can be used to slow the metabolism of ethylene glycol to decrease accumulation of toxic metabolites. B
Hemodialysis is an option for patients with severe renal dysfunction. C
Patients with severe metabolic acidosis, or hemodynamic/cardiopulmonary compromise should be admitted to the intensive care unit. C
The overall prognosis is typically favorable, even with mild to moderate renal impairment. C

background.definition: Ethylene glycol is a colorless, odorless chemical found in many household products, including antifreeze, de-icing products, detergents, paints, and cosmetics. When ingested in significant amounts, ethylene glycol may lead to nausea, vomiting, convulsions, stupor, shock, coma, and even death.

list.listitem: In 2021, 5747 cases of automotive ethylene glycol (antifreeze) ingestion were reported, the majority (3892) of which occurred among adults 20 years and older.

Most (4557) were unintentional, but nearly 10% (589) were intentional. Over 30% (1801) were treated in a health care facility; 2% resulted in major adverse health outcome. There were 9 reported deaths.
Ethylene glycol toxicity is caused by the ingestion of ethylene glycol or ethylene glycol-containing products; most commonly antifreeze.
Ethylene glycol is rapidly absorbed via the GI tract.
Approximately 80% of ethylene glycol is metabolized in the liver by alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase into glycolic acid, glyoxylic acid, and oxalic acid.

Oxalic acid can combine with calcium and result in hypocalcemia and calcium oxylate crystal deposition in the kidneys. If severe enough, this can progress to acute tubular necrosis and overt renal failure.
Serum chemistries and arterial blood gases should be checked in patients with altered mental status and known or suspected toxic ingestion. C
The Anion gap and osmolal gap should be calculated and used to narrow the differential diagnosis. B

Serum ethylene glycol, methanol, ethanol, and isopropyl alcohol levels should be checked in patients with elevated anion (ethylene glycol/methanol) and osmolal (ethylene glycol/isopropyl alcohol) gaps. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Anion and osmolal gap acidosis; urine crystals; increased creatinine; hypocalcemia

Differential.Differential_Name: Sepsis, lactic acidosis, acute renal failure
Differential.Differential_Features: Normal serum osmolal gap; elevated serum lactate
Visual changes; increased serum osmolal gap, formic acid, and methanol levels
Fruity breath; osmolal gap acidosis without anion gap; increased creatinine

list.listitem: Consider ethylene glycol toxicity in patients with altered mental status and metabolic acidosis of unknown origin.

Although ethylene glycol toxicity is described as having 3 distinct stages—CNS depression, cardiopulmonary complications, and renal dysfunction—there is considerable overlap of clinical findings among these stages, and they do not necessarily occur in order.
The most common presenting symptoms in the majority of patients include nausea, vomiting, slurred speech, ataxia, lethargy, and hyperventilation.

As toxicity becomes more severe, symptoms include agitation, confusion, cerebral edema, oliguric renal failure, hypotension, noninfectious pulmonary infiltrates, acute respiratory distress syndrome, cardiogenic pulmonary edema, coma, and death.
The absence of symptoms shortly after exposure does not represent the level of toxicity and should not be used as a triage criterion.
Order a serum metabolic panel, arterial blood gasses, and serum osmolality if ethylene glycol toxicity is suspected.

Use the metabolic panel to calculate the anion gap [Na − (Cl + HCO3)] and the osmolality (2[Na] + [BUN]/2.8 + [glucose]/18). Use the serum osmolality to calculate the osmolar gap (measured osmolarity - calculated osmolarity). The normal osmolar gap should be less than 10 mOsm/L.

In patients with anion gap metabolic acidosis and an elevated osmolal gap, order serum ethylene glycol, ethanol (normal ≤50 mg/L), methanol (normal ≤20 mg/dL), and isopropanol levels to assess for coingestion of other alcohols.
Order serum lactate (normal ≤2 mmol/L) and arterial blood gases to assess the degree of and cause of the metabolic acidosis.
Also order acetaminophen (normal ≤20 mg/mL, 132 mmol/L; check nomogram) and salicylate levels (normal ≤25 mg/dL, 1.8 mmol/L) to assess for common co-ingestions.

Serum ethylene glycol concentrations of greater than 20 mg/dL (3.2 mmol/L) are most often associated with clinically significant toxicity (renal failure, seizures, altered mental status), and if present, inhibition of alcohol dehydrogenase with fomepizole is suggested. Ethylene glycol ingestions of 1 g/kg are thought to be lethal.
Urine evaluation with a Wood's lamp can reveal envelope-shaped or needle-shaped calcium oxalate crystals (microscopic analysis) or positive fluorescence in ethylene glycol ingestions.

Patients with suspected ethylene glycol exposure should be immediately referred to the emergency department regardless of suspected dose. Obtain the amount, concentration, and time of ingestion; objective proof of the specific ingested product will assist the poison control center.

Order chemistries and calculate the anion gap and the osmolal gap. An anion-gap metabolic acidosis AND osmolal gap are both present in ethylene glycol toxicity (the osmolal gap may normalize late in the ingestion because of decreased substrate).
See for a suggested approach to evaluation.
Hemodynamic, renal, and/or cardiopulmonary compromise should be supported with vasoactive agents and ventilatory support in an intensive care unit. C
Reverse metabolic acidosis by using bicarbonate infusions. C

Fomepizole is the agent of choice to inhibit the metabolism of ethylene glycol. B Ethanol administered intravenously can be used to inhibit the metabolism of ethylene glycol B and is the preferred agent in first-trimester pregnancy or allergy to fomepizole. C
Hemodialysis in ethylene glycol toxicity is typically used when renal function is severely impaired and is not solely based on the severity of metabolic acidosis. C

Sodium bicarbonate infusion (see below) should be administered if the metabolic acidosis is severe (base deficit >10); particularly, early in the ingestion prior to administration of an alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor.

Inhibition of alcohol dehydrogenase is central in preventing continued metabolism of ethylene glycol to its toxic metabolites. This can be achieved by the administration of ethanol or fomepizole infusions (see below) as both are preferred substrates for alcohol dehydrogenase. These agents should be initiated in patients with metabolic acidosis and/or renal dysfunction with ethylene glycols levels greater than 20 mg/dL (3.2 mmol/L), or in nonacidotic patients with ethylene glycol levels greater than 40 mg/dL (6.5 mmol/L).

The typical elimination half-life of ethylene glycol is approximately 6 hours. Fomepizole, a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase, prevents the metabolism of ethylene glycol to its toxic metabolites, thereby increasing the elimination time for intact ethylene glycol.

Additional inhibitors of alcohol dehydrogenase are methanol, ethanol, and isopropanol because they are preferred substrates over ethylene glycol. Coingestion of these substances may minimize ethylene glycol toxicity, while increasing the elimination time.
Fomepizole dosing: 15 mg/kg IV loading dose followed by 10 mg/kg IV every 12 hours for 4 doses. If the patient is symptomatic at 48 hours, increase subsequent doses to 15 mg/kg IV every 12 hours.
Ethanol dosing: 8 mL/kg IV of a 10% ethanol solution loading dose followed by an infusion of 1.5 mL/kg per hour to maintain serum ethanol level at 100 to 150 mg/dL.

For patients with a pH of less than 7.3, start sodium bicarbonate: 1 to 2 mEq/kg bolus followed by infusion of 132 mEq in 1 liter dextrose 5% at 200 to 250 cc per hour. Normalize pH to minimize formate access to the CNS and optic toxicity.

Although no data suggest superiority of one antidote over another, fomepizole is less labor intensive, has more prolonged action, requires less laboratory support, and does not cause CNS suppression. However, it is less widely available and significantly more expensive than other antidotes.

Although pyridoxine (50 mg IV) and thiamine (100 mg IV) are frequently given to enhance metabolism of glycolic acid, the evidence supporting such practices is insufficient, and routine use is not recommended.

General treatment of ethylene glycol toxicity is supportive, with the implementation of additional therapy based on the level of metabolic acidosis and severity of ingestion. Begin airway, breathing, and circulatory support in any patient demonstrating cardiopulmonary compromise. Provide endotracheal intubation, IV fluids, and vasopressor agents to maintain mean arterial blood pressure at greater than 65 mm Hg and urine output greater than 0.5 mL/kg.
Contact United States Poison Control Network at 1-800-222-1222 or a WHO International Poison control Center.

If a patient presents within 1 hour of ingestion, consider gastric lavage/aspiration. Because activated charcoal has limited binding of ethylene glycol it is not indicated unless coingestion of additional substances is suspected. Gastrointestinal decontamination in the out-of-hospital setting is not recommended and transportation to an emergency department should not be delayed by decontamination procedures.

Isolated hypocalcemia should not be treated because of the increased risk of calcium oxalate precipitation in tissues. However, hypocalcemia-induced seizures should be treated with IV calcium gluconate.

Hemodialysis can be used to remove ethylene glycol. It is guided by the severity of renal dysfunction, not the severity of metabolic acidosis or ethylene glycol levels. Hemodialysis should be continued until serum ethylene glycol levels are less than 20 mg/dL. If ethylene glycol levels are not readily available, hemodialysis should be continued for 8 hours after resolution of metabolic acidosis.

A systematic review by the the EXtracorporeal TReatments In Poisoning (EXTRIP) workgroup, based mostly on very low-quality evidence, recommends the following for ethylene glycol poisoning:
Perform hemodialysis if ethanol is used and ethylene glycol (EG) concentration is >50 mml/L (>310 mg/dL) or osmol gap >50. In the absence of an antidote (alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor), perform hemodialysis if EG concentration is >10 mmol/L (>62 mg/dL) or osmol gap >10. Perform hemodialysis if glycolate concentration >12 mmol/L or anion gap >27 mmol/L. Perform hemodialysis if there are severe clinical features (eg, coma, seizures, acute kidney injury stage 2 or 3). If available, intermittent hemodialysis is preferred over continuous renal replacement therapy. Stop hemodialysis when anion gap is <18 mmol/L.

Admit patients to an intensive care unit when metabolic acidosis is severe (base deficit >20 mM) or when they present with manifestations of severe toxicity (eg, lethargy, hypotension, adult respiratory distress syndrome, pulmonary edema).
The prognosis is generally favorable in patients diagnosed and treated early in the course of ingestion, even in the presence of severe acidosis. C
Renal dysfunction typically returns to normal within 1 month. C
A large osmolal or anion gap at presentation has been associated with increased mortality.B
Serum glycolic acid concentrations may predict mortality, with a sensitivity of 85% and specificity of 54% at a threshold of 990 mg/dL.B

Although the diagnosis of ethylene glycol poisoning in pregnant and nonpregnant women is similar, clinicians treating poisoned pregnant patients must exercise caution, especially in the first trimester of pregnancy.

Fomepizole is not recommended in first-trimester pregnancies. Despite the well-known adverse effects of ethanol on fetal development in the first trimester, a 2- to 3-day course of ethanol therapy is likely less toxic than fomepizole.
